[[Image:Prosopis pubescens inflorescence 2003-06-02.jpg|thumb|right|200px|[[Flower]] [[Raceme|spikes]]]]
'''''Strombocarpa pubescens''''' (formerly '''''Prosopis pubescens'''''), commonly known as '''screwbean mesquite''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PRPU|taxon=Prosopis pubescens|accessdate=14 October 2015}}</ref>  is a species of [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] in the pea family, [[Fabaceae]], that is native to the [[southwestern United States]] ([[Texas]], [[Arizona]], [[New Mexico]], [[California]], southern [[Nevada]] and [[Utah]]) and northern [[Mexico]] ([[Baja California]], [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Coahuila]], [[Sonora]]).<ref name=powo/><ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN | accessdate=2010-01-03}}</ref>

==Description==
This plant grows to about {{convert|7|m|ft|abbr=on}}. It has light brown [[Bark (botany)|bark]], usually short, straight [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]] 1 to 3 centimeters long, twice-[[Leaf shape|compound]] [[Leaf|leaves]], and numerous small yellowish [[flower]]s appearing in elongate [[Raceme|spikes]]. The tightly twisted seedpods ([[legume]]s) are up to 5 centimeters long and very much resemble turned [[screw]]s. This [[Morphology (biology)|morphology]] may have been an [[evolution]]ary [[Plant defense against herbivory|defense]] against [[Seed predation|seed predators]] such as [[bean weevil]]s (Bruchinae). The seeds [[germination|germinate]] after being [[scarification (botany)|scarified]] in the digestive tracts of animals that eat them. The plant also grows in a clockwise spiral.<ref name=fs>{{cite web|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/propub/all.html|title=Species: Prosopis pubescens|work=fs.fed.us|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210211205404/http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/propub/all.html |accessdate=4 August 2015|archive-date=11 February 2021 }}</ref>

==Habitat==
It is found along streams and valleys in [[desert]]s, particularly in damp or [[Soil salinity|saline]] [[soil]]. It grows alongside common plants of this habitat type, such as arrowweed (''[[Pluchea sericea]]'') and [[tamarix|tamarisks]].<ref name=fs/> It can be found on [[Sink (geography)|playas]] and other areas of [[alkali soils|alkaline substrates]].<ref name=fs/> This and other mesquite species are dominant plants in the [[Mesquite Bosque]]-mesquite woodlands, a common habitat type in the desert southwest region.<ref name=fs/>

Many types of animals readily eat the seedpods, including several bird and rodent species and [[coyote]]s.<ref name=fs/> Many species of birds nest and roost in the trees, and small mammals find shelter in thicketlike stands.<ref name=fs/>

==Uses==

===Food===
Like those of other ''Strombocarpa'', ''Neltuma'' and ''Prosopis'' species, Screwbean Mesquite has nutritious [[Legume|seedpods]] that can be eaten.<ref name=Audubon/> The [[Pima people|Pimas]] cooked the pods in dirt-covered pits over intervals of a few days.<ref>{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |authorlink=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |page=568}}</ref> Mesquite is a traditional [[Native American food]] source, being used to make meal, cakes and syrup.<ref name=Audubon/> Used as a staple food for centuries by desert dwellers, this high [[protein]] meal contains good quantities of [[calcium]], [[magnesium]], [[potassium]], [[iron]] and [[zinc]], and is rich in the [[amino acid]] [[lysine]] as well. Mesquite is high in [[Dietary fiber|fiber]], moderate in [[sugar]], and 8% protein. It has a sweet, rich, [[molasses]]-like flavor with a hint of [[caramel]] which blends well into [[smoothie]]s or other drinks, especially those made with [[Cocoa powder|cacao]] and [[maca]]. The fruits may be used as a [[coffee substitute]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?3691,4179,4181|title=UC/JEPS: Jepson Manual treatment for PROSOPIS pubescens|work=berkeley.edu|accessdate=4 August 2015}}</ref>

[[File:Prosopis_pubescens_dry_seeds.jpg|thumb|200px|Dried seed pods]]

===Wood===
Native Americans found Screwbean wood valuable for building, for making tools and weapons, and as [[firewood]].<ref name=fs/> The wood is durable and considered attractive, and it may be used in [[woodworking]].<ref name=fs/> Some Native Americans also used the root bark to prepare a treatment for wounds.<ref name=Audubon>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-date=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0394507614 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=501}}</ref>
